Southwest Research Institute® U.S. DOE Award Number DE-FE0032301 Public Version - 20 - DE-FE0032301 Final Report Programmatically, the project provides DOE and the broader research community with a proven framework for integrating plasma-assisted reforming into natural-gas combustion systems. The results demonstrate that methane leak reductions can be achieved through fuel reactivity modification rather than traditional aftertreatment, representing a fundamentally different approach to methane mitigation. 5.3 Conclusions This project successfully demonstrated the technical feasibility and performance advantages of a pulsed plasma fuel reformer for methane-leak reduction in natural-gas engines. The work advanced the system from concept design through engine-scale validation within the two-year performance period. Key conclusions include: 1. Stable and efficient plasma operation was achieved across all test environments, from laboratory to engine-scale conditions, with no recurring electrical or thermal faults after final design modifications. 2. Partial methane decomposition within the plasma reformer generated hydrogen and light hydrocarbons that enhanced combustion efficiency and reduced methane slip without adversely affecting engine stability. 3. Energy efficiency approached thermodynamic limits, with low-flow methane-conversion energy of approximately 74 kJ/mol, which closely approximates the theoretical enthalpy of decomposition. 4. Combustion smoothness improved, as indicated by reduced peak heat-release rates and more uniform pressure profiles, suggesting a more evenly distributed burn that can result in lower mechanical stress. 5. Methane-leak reductions ranged from 1–2 percent with pre-chamber reformation on large- bore AJAX 2802 ULE engine and 6–27 percent on the high-speed Cummins X15N, confirming performance scalability across different combustion regimes. 6. Reformer power consumption remained well below 1 percent of engine output, meeting the project target, as defined by practical limits for industrial adoption. 7. Minimal electromagnetic interference (EMI) or control-system disruptions occurred during integrated operation, validating compatibility with modern engine electronics. These findings indicate that plasma-assisted fuel reforming is a promising, low-energy approach for reducing methane slip in natural-gas engines. While additional endurance and field testing are necessary to assess long-term performance, the results demonstrate the potential for practical deployment across a range of stationary and mobile natural-gas applications. 5.4 Future Work and Commercialization Outlook Future development efforts are planned to focus on improving the reformer’s operational durability, enhancing fuel composition control, and validating long-term performance under representative field conditions.
